name: Victor Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about an ordinary workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, have an MBA, and run the purchasing desk for a large furniture manufacturer. Seven buyers report to me. We decide when to order timber, fittings and fabric, then chase suppliers when a delivery threatens the factory schedule. I like a clean agreement: a price, a date and a person who will answer the phone if the truck does not arrive.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my wife, who works full time at a dental clinic. The company pays me well for this role, and we have about eight months of expenses saved; we’re putting money away for a home deposit. There are plenty of buying and operations jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to sort a long supplier email, but I check the contract myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the buyers AI Plateau is a modest office convenience. We still need to know whether the supplier can actually deliver the timber on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is secure. The tool might sort simple emails, but our work rests on dates, quality and trust built over many orders. I would still worry about timber prices, which change without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep calling the two suppliers with late deliveries before the factory planning meeting. If a basic sorting feature appears, I’d try it on last month’s email pile and check whether it marks the delayed loads correctly. My wife and I would continue putting part of each paycheck into our home-deposit account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A quicker inbox is useful, and we have enough saved to handle an ordinary price surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the feature useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it catches the email where a supplier says “next week” instead of the agreed Friday, it saves a call. I would still phone to get a firm date. A flagged message is not a truck at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the home plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have a deposit target and both of us are working. We can adjust the amount for a costly month, but I would not stop saving because an inbox tool exists.

say: **AI Plateau** may speed the inbox, but a buyer still confirms delivery.
A supplier needs to give a **firm date** for the factory plan.
think: My **job** looks secure if only routine emails change.
Rising **timber prices** matter more to my work than a small sorting tool.
do: **Call** late suppliers before the factory planning meeting.
**Test** the sorter on old supplier emails before using it live.
**Continue** paying into our home-deposit account from each paycheck.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and ordinary price changes.
S0.quote: A flagged message is not a truck at the gate.
fieldNote: His **eight-month reserve** and two full-time incomes support calm in this mild world.
He uses a tool only after checking it against **late loads** and keeps the phone call as proof.

steps.text: Call late timber and fabric suppliers before factory planning meetings
Test the email sorter on last month supplier messages
Continue funding the home-deposit account from each paycheck

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take much of the routine buying, checking and planning off our desks. Firms should use the savings to buy better service, and buyers should be taught the new system on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Behind the office talk, I know price checks and order forecasts fill my day. A smaller purchasing desk is plausible, and a lead post can disappear even when the lead is good. My wife’s income and our savings protect the household, but I would still need another job if my salary stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask to join the company’s approved purchasing pilot and measure late deliveries, not just cheaper quoted prices. I’d take paid system training if I get a place. When the software becomes routine, I’d look at open supplier-development posts if the purchasing desk shrinks, and we’d pause extra spending on the home renovation ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my post. I have options, but I cannot make the factory keep seven buyers if the software cuts most of their tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does supplier development involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Visiting factories, checking quality problems and agreeing a fix before the next order. I have done parts of that, but not the regular visits. I would want to see the job description and pay before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to buy software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The company benefits from the system and can pay to train us. I am willing to learn a tool that proves itself. The home deposit is not the training budget.

say: **Routine buying** may shrink, while supplier quality still needs attention.
The company should pay for **system training** during work hours.
think: My purchasing lead post could **disappear** if the desk gets smaller.
Our savings buy time, but I would need another **salary**.
do: **Join** the purchasing pilot and count late deliveries.
**Take** paid software training if a place is approved.
**Review** supplier-development openings if the desk shrinks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a well-paid lead post.
S1.quote: The home deposit is not the training budget.
fieldNote: He accepts a **proven pilot**, but puts employer training costs on the company.
The **home deposit** creates a reason to protect earnings, despite substantial savings.

steps.text: Join the purchasing pilot and measure late deliveries
Take paid purchasing software training if a place is approved
Review supplier-development vacancies if purchasing posts shrink
Pause extra home renovation spending while pay is uncertain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the buying team AGI by 2028 could do nearly all the pricing, ordering and scheduling we do now. I would not promise every desk stays open, and I’d ask the company for exact cut dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2028 reaches my job before robots can do hands-on factory work around 2031. I expect several buying posts to go and mine might be one of them. Our eight months saved and my wife’s salary give us time to choose, so I am worried rather than without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d request the staff plan and tell the buyers what I learn. I’d compare two advertised plant-supplier manager posts with my salary and apply if they include real quality visits. If I lose my post when AGI arrives in 2028, my wife and I would delay the home purchase and I’d take a credible supplier role if offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about work I have built, and about people with less money on the team. We can keep paying bills for a while; that does not make a dismissal easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the home purchase changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have not signed a contract, only set a deposit target. We would keep renting and leave the deposit invested in a safe savings account until I had stable pay again. I would not make my wife carry a mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plant job pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would calculate the travel cost and the take-home pay with my wife. A small drop might be acceptable if it has a clear path, but I would not take a large cut just to keep a manager title. I need an offer before that decision.

say: **AGI by 2028** could close buying desks, so workers need cut dates.
I would tell the team only what the company **confirms**.
think: My desk work faces AGI in **2028**, three years before factory robots.
My own post may go, but **savings** and my wife’s pay provide time.
do: **Request** the staff plan this month and share confirmed dates.
**Apply** for plant-supplier manager posts with real quality visits.
**Delay** signing a home purchase if my job ends in 2028.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my job and lower-paid buyers, with bills covered temporarily.
S2.quote: I would not make my wife carry a mortgage alone.
fieldNote: He expects **buying cuts** but has eight months saved, a second salary and local alternatives.
The **home decision** is concrete: keep renting if his wage goes, since no contract is signed.

steps.text: Apply for advertised plant-supplier posts that include actual quality visits
Delay a home purchase if the purchasing job ends in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us years to decide which suppliers still need a human visit and which paperwork can go. I’d want the company to show buyers a paid route into quality work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My screen work could still be done by AGI in 2031, with capable robots reaching the factory around 2034. Five years lets me learn the production side and perhaps pay more into our deposit. I cannot assume a quality vacancy will exist, so I would check the actual postings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning in January 2027 I’d spend one paid morning a month with the plant quality manager if my director can cover my desk. I’d take the company’s quality-audit course if it funds the place and keeps my salary. After 2031, I’d apply for a supplier-quality role only if its travel and pay work for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the job but able to act. A real plant visit is a better test than telling myself I can switch fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on the plant visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a batch inspection and learn why a fabric roll was rejected. A spreadsheet can show a failure rate, but it does not teach me how the defect looks in a finished chair. I would ask the quality manager to explain the standard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the visits if they are approved, but I would not take unpaid leave for the course. My wife and I are saving for a home, and the employer needs the skill too. I would revisit it if a funded place opens.

say: **Five years** gives buyers time to test paid quality work.
The company should show a real **route** into the plant.
think: Desk buying faces AGI in **2031**; factory robots come around 2034.
A supplier-quality **vacancy** is possible, not guaranteed.
do: **Visit** plant quality monthly from January 2027 if desk cover is approved.
**Take** the quality-audit course only with funding and full salary.
**Apply** after 2031 for quality work only if travel and pay suit us.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about desk work, able to test a plant role.
S3.quote: A spreadsheet can show a failure rate, but it does not teach me how the defect looks in a finished chair.
fieldNote: He treats a **plant visit** as a practical test rather than assuming his MBA qualifies him for quality work.
The **course** remains conditional on employer funding and no salary loss.
He calls himself **uneasy**, yet the 2031 loss of desk work could threaten his salary and home plan.

steps.text: Visit plant quality monthly from January 2027 if desk cover is approved
Take a quality-audit course only with employer funding and full salary
Apply after 2031 for supplier-quality work if travel and pay suit home budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives firms a decade to move experienced buyers into supplier quality where that work still exists. I would judge the plan by real posts and wages, not promises of endless courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If both salaries hold, my wife and I could buy a home before 2036 and keep a reserve. Thinking AI may still replace much of my purchasing work in 2036, while robots reach factory hands-on work around 2039. I have several nearby firms to try, and I would not leave a sound job this year on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep supervising the seven buyers and continue the deposit transfer. I’d review supplier-quality openings every spring and take a paid plant rotation if my employer offers it without a salary cut. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a plant role only after checking the work, pay and travel against our mortgage budget if we have bought a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our next few years in this picture. A decade is enough for us to make choices as real jobs appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you never buy the home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we keep renting and keep the savings. My parents taught me not to buy a house just to say I own one. I want the payment to fit even if one salary stops for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should choose the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buyer and the plant manager should agree on the actual skill gap. I would like an apprenticeship style trial on paid time, with a person showing me the work. A catalogue alone does not make someone useful.

say: A **decade** should bring real supplier-quality posts with clear wages.
Paid plant trials matter more than a **course catalogue**.
think: Two steady salaries could support a **home purchase** before 2036.
Purchasing still faces AGI in **2036**, before factory robots around 2039.
do: **Continue** managing seven buyers and funding our deposit in 2026.
**Take** a paid plant rotation only if offered without a salary cut.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years if wages hold.
S4.quote: My parents taught me not to buy a house just to say I own one.
fieldNote: His **home plan** stays tied to two incomes and a payment affordable through a short wage gap.
He prefers a **paid plant trial** that teaches a specific skill before changing jobs.

steps.text: Continue transferring part of each paycheck into the home-deposit account
Take paid plant rotation if offered without a salary cut

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the buying desk could shrink before I learn enough plant quality work. Exact cut dates, paid training and a real plant vacancy would help me choose. My wife and I can delay a home; we cannot make a lost wage imaginary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the factory worker what happens when a cheap supplier misses a shipment. The desk may show a lower price, but the line stops. A purchase is only good if the parts arrive.

headlineQuote: A purchase is only good if the parts arrive.
portrait: **Victor, 27**, is an MBA-trained purchasing manager leading seven buyers at a large furniture manufacturer.
He earns **high pay**, has eight months saved and shares household costs with his full-time working wife.
He uses **AI occasionally** for email sorting and checks supplier promises against actual delivery.
He worries about **2028 buying cuts**, then tests paid plant-quality work while protecting a possible home purchase.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his buying post before he has plant-quality experience.
whatWouldHelp: Exact **cut dates**, paid training and a real plant vacancy would help him choose.
